AITA for leaving to see my GF when my sister told me not to when she was "in charge"? | My mom is gone for a class thing in another state, and my dad is on a business trip so its just me, my sister and my brother all alone in the house. My sister is 18, I am 17 and my brother is 12, I don't know why but my parents still felt the need to leave my sister "in charge" while they were both gone. My sister lets the power go to her head and while she can generally make my little brother obey her she has a tougher time with me. On Sunday I was gonna go out with my GF for dinner, and my sister stopped me saying that I can't leave. When asked its cause "she said so", I laughed at that and I thought she was joking but she just kept looking and I knew it was a joke. I told her she can boss (little brother's name) around but she can't boss me, and I went out with my GF. I guess my younger brother heard all the commotion and called mom saying we were "fighting" and when I came home and my mom called me she said that I'm grounded and have to dow what my sister says cause she's "in charge". I protested as best as I could but she wasn't having it and grounded me for disobeying my sister who is a pseudo parent while they are away. I just dropped it cause its not worth arguing any point with my mom. AITA here? EDIT:My brother told me afterwards that he was the one that told mom, I forgave him cause I mean I can't be mad at that little turd for too long

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: 0 ( **Not AITA** — you're not the asshole here. Here's why:) ### **Key Reasoning:** - **Your sister's " authority" was arbitrary and overstepping.** Being " in charge" while parents are away **does not** mean she can arbitrarily forbid a 17-year-old from going out with their girlfriend. " She said so" is not a valid rule — it's just her personal opinion. True " in charge" responsibilities ( e.g., " no parties, no strangers over, no curfew violations") are usually defined by parents *in advance*. If your parents didn explicitly say " you must obey every command from your sister," her " order" was unreasonable. - *Example*: If your sister had said " Mom said no one can leave the house after 9 PM," that would be a clear rule. But " she said so" is just her being controlling — not a legitimate authority. - **You're 17 — nearly an adult.** At 17, you're old enough to make decisions about your social life *unless* there's a specific, pre agreed upon rule ( e.g., " no going out without checking in with your sister"). The fact that she " can boss your brother around" ( a 12-year-old) but not you is **completely normal** — older siblings don't have inherent authority over younger siblings' personal choices, especially when those choices are age-appropriate ( e.g., a dinner date with a girlfriend). - **Your mom overreacted.** grounding you for " disobeying your sister" without asking *why* she said no or whether there was a real rule is unfair. If your mom had said " Mom specifically told us no one can leave the house," that would be different. But since she didn't, her grounding was based on your sister's *self appointed* authority — not actual parental instructions. - *This is a common AITA pattern*: When a " in charge" sibling makes up rules on the spot, the younger sibling isn't the asshole for questioning it. The *real* issue is the sister overstepping and the mom not verifying the situation. - **Your brother's role is irrelevant.** He called Mom about " fighting," but it was just a disagreement over a personal choice — not a physical fight or serious violation. Forgiving him is mature, but it doesn't change the core issue: **you didn't do anything wrong** by leaving when there was no clear, pre established rule against it. ### **Why This Matters:** - **True " in charge" means managing the house safely** ( e.g., " no a, no leaving the house unattended"), not micromanaging a 17-year-old's social life. - **Parents should clarify rules *before* they leave** — e.g., " no going out after 10 PM," " no unsupervised guests," etc. Vague " she's in charge" without specifics is a setup for conflict. - **You were reasonable to push back** on an arbitrary " order." If you had obeyed without question, you'd be normalizing a sibling's overreach — which is *not* healthy. ### **What to Do Next:** - **Talk to your parents calmly:** * " Mom, I respect that you trust my sister to watch the house, but I need clear rules. If you want me to check in with her before going out, just tell me that upfront. ' She said so' isn't a rule — it's her personal opinion. I'm 17, and I deserve to know what's expected of me."* - **Ask your sister to be specific next time:** * " If you're going to tell me I can't go out, tell me *why* — is it a curfew? A safety thing? If not, I'm not going to follow arbitrary ' orders' from you."* **Bottom line:** You're not the asshole. Your sister overstepped, and your mom should have investigated before grounding you. **True responsibility is about clear rules — not arbitrary power trips.** 💡 *(P.S. If this happens again, document the rules *before* your parents leave next time. " Mom, can you text me exactly what I'm allowed to do while you're gone? I want to make sure I follow the rules correctly." — that's mature and proactive.)*
